idiom_name: two buffer instances + a single atomic swap (index, pointer or reference exchange; copy when consumers cannot be re-pointed)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: instantiate the buffer twice, designate one as current (read-only to the outside) and one as next (private to the writer), and complete every update cycle with exactly one swap operation. The swap is the whole synchronization story: make it a single atomic store of a pointer, reference or index with release semantics, or a critical section when several fields move together, and have readers load it with acquire semantics (or through the language's volatile/atomic snapshot primitive) before touching the buffer. If consumers need a fixed address (DMA, GPU front buffer, memory-mapped display), swap by copying the finished next buffer over the current one under the same synchronization and accept the O(size) cost. Keep the pair monolithic when possible so one swap covers everything; if the state is spread over a collection, give every object the same current offset or wrap them in one owning structure. Never write into a buffer while it is current, and never let readers keep a pointer into a buffer across a swap.
code_sketch:
class Buffered:
    buffers[2]; current = 0
    def next():  return buffers[1 - current]   # writer's private scratch
    def read():  return buffers[current]       # readers see a whole frame
    def swap():  current = 1 - current         # the only atomic step

frame():
    b = next(); b.clear(); render_into(b)
    swap()                                    # publish the finished frame
pitfalls: Swapping with a plain store while readers are active: without release/acquire ordering (or a lock) a reader can see the new address before the buffer contents are visible.
Allowing the writer to keep modifying the buffer it just published - the snapshot contract is what makes the swap sufficient.
Readers caching pointers into the buffer across a swap and then using the recycled generation.
Assuming the back buffer still holds the previous frame: with alternation it holds data from two frames ago unless you copy.
Distributing the buffered state across many objects and then swapping them one by one - the swap is no longer atomic as a whole.
Swap aliasing: writing the next buffer while the reader is mid-read on the current buffer — on weakly ordered CPUs the reader may observe stale or reordered writes from the writer's buffer.
Buffer reuse after disconnect: when consumers disconnect and reconnect, they may hold a stale reference into the old buffer generation and observe a freed or repurposed memory region.

Wrong move: running double buffering with vsync and expecting minimum latency -> the finished frame idles in the back buffer until the next vertical blank, adding up to a full refresh interval of input lag -> instead use a lower-latency present mode (mailbox, adaptive sync) or triple buffering so the freshest completed frame is always the one presented.

Wrong move: hand-rolling a ping-pong pair underneath a platform that already flips (D3D/DXGI swap chain, AWT BufferStrategy, ALSA PCM periods, STM32 DMA DBM) -> the software buffer competes with the hardware's own swap, adding a copy or an extra queued frame of latency -> instead drive the hardware double-buffer facility directly and treat its present call or completion interrupt as the swap.

Wrong move: in a DMA ping-pong setup, processing whichever buffer the code last wrote instead of consulting the current-target indicator (STM32 CT bit, ALSA period event) -> software reads a buffer the DMA engine is still filling, yielding torn samples that look like a corruption bug -> instead derive the processed buffer strictly from the hardware's target/period flag and hand ownership over only at the transfer-complete interrupt.
sources: Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns (2014), Double Buffer: buffered class, pointer re-point vs. data copy, monolithic vs. per-object granularity.
Wikipedia, Multiple buffering: double buffering, page flipping, swap chains, vsync.
Khronos Group, Vulkan Swapchain Images: double vs. triple buffering decision tree, VK_PRESENT_MODE_FIFO_KHR vs. MAILBOX_KHR.

Dmitry Vyukov, bounded MPMC queue: the canonical lock-free multi-producer multi-consumer queue used as the foundation of crossbeam-channel; compare-and-swap-free fast path with acquire/release memory ordering.
geronimo-iia, spsc-ring: sequence-number protocol SPSC ring buffer, cache-line padding, compile-time Send-but-not-Sync contract.
